statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether psilocybin changes personality. In two small studies with no comparison group for the change, self-rated Openness to experience on the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (T scores: population mean 50, SD 10) was a few points higher 1 to 3 months after psilocybin with preparation and support than each person's own score before; the one randomized comparison of personality in these trials found no difference, no paper checked a change against behaviour, and the two papers disagree on whether the change followed the experience. In 52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, unpaid volunteers pooled from two double-blind trials at Johns Hopkins (mean age 46; 54% with postgraduate degrees; 90% regularly taking part in religious or spiritual activities; screening Openness 65.4 and 62.7), Openness was 2.8 T points higher 1 to 2 months after the high-dose session (psilocybin 30 mg/70 kg, study condition; F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023), Neuroticism, Extroversion, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness did not change detectably, and in the 30 whose first session was placebo, methylphenidate or a low psilocybin dose Openness did not change after that session (p = 0.48), though the two changes were never compared with each other (MacLean et al., 2011). The rise was in the 30 who met the criterion for a 'complete mystical experience' (+5.7, p = 0.002), not in the other 22 (−1.2), and it correlated with the session's mystical score (r = 0.42); individual changes ranged from about −12 to +36 T points, about 17 of the 51 visible points in the paper's figure lie below zero (about a third of the volunteers scored lower; editors' reading), and without the three largest rises the other 49 would average about +1.3 (editors' approximate calculation, (2.8 × 52 − 84) / 49). At a mean of 16 months the complete-mystical group was 4.2 points above its screening score at p = 0.050 (0.0503 by the editors' calculation) and the others 0.3 below; the change for all participants together was not reported. In the earlier trial that supplied 35 of these volunteers, the randomized comparison of 15 people given psilocybin first with 15 given methylphenidate first found no difference in any personality factor 2 months later (no values printed; Griffiths et al., 2006, as its checked study card reports), a result MacLean et al. do not mention. In 19 adults with treatment-resistant depression given psilocybin 10 mg and then 25 mg a week later with psychological support in an open-label study in London (Erritzoe et al., 2018; its authors include MacLean et al.'s first author), Neuroticism fell from T 76.6 to 70.9 (p = 0.002), Extraversion rose from 31.1 to 37.6 (p < 0.001) and Openness from 52.7 to 57.6 (p = 0.012) at 3 months, Conscientiousness rose at trend level (p = 0.086) and Agreeableness did not change; Neuroticism, Extraversion and Conscientiousness moved from far outside the norms towards them, and the authors say it is hard to infer that the changes, particularly in Neuroticism and Extraversion, are traits rather than states. The Openness rise did not differ between the 7 patients whose depression responded and the 12 whose did not, and no 'peak experience' score related to it, whereas insightfulness during the session went with the Neuroticism and Extraversion changes in uncorrected, exploratory correlations (r = −0.47 and 0.54). All scores are self-ratings by people who knew, or could probably tell, that they had taken psilocybin, in volunteers drawn to a psilocybin study or to a psychedelic treatment; in the 2006 trial, three people close to each volunteer rated a small positive change in behaviour and attitudes after psilocybin (Griffiths et al., 2006, as its card reports), but no paper read related such ratings, or any behaviour, to the personality scores. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Can psilocybin change your personality? It has not been shown. In two small studies, people rated themselves a few points more open to experience 1 to 3 months after psilocybin with preparation and support than before, on a scale where the average adult scores 50 and the usual spread is 10 points: 2.8 points in 52 healthy, mostly religious or spiritual volunteers, and 4.9 points in 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression. Neither study compared the change with people who did not get psilocybin, and in the one comparison of this kind in the same trials, 15 people who had psilocybin first and 15 who had a stimulant first did not differ 2 months later. In the volunteers, the rise came from those who had a 'complete' mystical experience, and about a third of all the volunteers scored lower afterwards; more than a year later that group was still about 4 points up, a result right on the edge of chance. The patients also rated themselves less anxious and more sociable as their depression lifted, which the researchers say may reflect mood rather than lasting traits, and the two studies disagree on whether the change followed the experience. Neither study checked the scores against how people behave.
population: 52 healthy, hallucinogen-naive, unpaid volunteers recruited by community flyers for a study of states of consciousness brought about by psilocybin (35 from a 2006 trial and 17 from a 2011 trial at Johns Hopkins; mean age 46; 22 men and 30 women, editors' sum; 54% with postgraduate degrees; 90% regularly taking part in religious services, discussion groups, prayer or meditation; screening Openness T 65.4 and 62.7); in the 2006 trial, 30 volunteers randomized to drug order (15 per order); and 19 analysed of 20 adults with moderate to severe treatment-resistant unipolar depression in an open-label study in London (6 women, 13 men; mean age 44.7; five had tried a psychedelic before).
exposure: Psilocybin by mouth with preparation and support, as study conditions only: one session at 30 mg/70 kg (in the 2011 trial within four ascending or descending doses with a placebo session), lying down with an eye mask and music, after at least 8 hours of meetings with the session monitors; in the open-label study, 10 mg and then 25 mg a week later, eyes closed with music and two therapists, with integration visits afterwards.
comparator: Each person's own personality scores before (screening or baseline), with no concurrent comparison of change in either main study; within the healthy volunteers, people with and without a 'complete mystical experience' (not randomized) and, separately, change after a first session of placebo, methylphenidate or psilocybin 5 mg/70 kg; in the 2006 trial, people given psilocybin first against people given methylphenidate first (randomized; no values printed).
outcome: Self-rated personality on the NEO Personality Inventory-Revised (240 items; five domains of six facets; T scores from combined-sex norms), 1 to 2 months after the session and about 14 months after the last session (a mean of 16 months after the high-dose session) in the healthy volunteers, and 3 months after in the patients; no behavioural measure and no ratings of personality by others.
magnitude: MacLean et al. (2011), 52 volunteers, screening to 1–2 months: Openness +2.8 T points, F(1, 51) = 5.47, p = 0.023, partial eta squared 0.10 (editors' calculation: within-person standardized change about 0.32, √(5.47/52)); Neuroticism −0.5 (p = 0.62), Extroversion +0.8 (p = 0.38), Agreeableness +1.7 (F = 2.31, printed p = 0.16; 0.13 by the editors' calculation), Conscientiousness −0.9 (p = 0.28). After a first session without high-dose psilocybin (30): F(1, 29) = 0.52, p = 0.48. Complete mystical experience (30) against not (22): F(1, 50) = 9.32, p = 0.004; +5.7 (t(29) = 3.44, p = 0.002) against −1.2 (t(21) = 0.87, p = 0.39). Mystical score and Openness change r = 0.42, p = 0.002 (editors' 95% CI about 0.17 to 0.62, Fisher z). Follow-up (mean 16 months): complete group +4.2, F(1, 29) = 4.17, p = 0.050 (0.0503 by the editors' calculation); others (21) −0.3, p = 0.86; all participants not reported. Figure 1 (editors' reading): changes from about −12 to +36, about 17 of 51 visible points below zero; about +1.3 without the three largest (editors' approximate calculation). Griffiths et al. risk_of_bias.note: The estimates are before-and-after changes in self-ratings: the parent trials' randomization does not protect them (RoB 2 high on the MacLean card), and the patient study has no control group (ROBINS-I critical). The volunteers could probably tell when they had the high dose, were unpaid, motivated and mostly spiritually active, and their expectations were not measured; the mystical-experience groups were formed by what happened in the session; the patients knew they had psilocybin, their depression was lifting, and their extreme baseline scores leave room for regression towards the norms. MacLean et al. describe every high-dose session as blinded, but the 2006 report, as its checked card gives it, says 6 of its 36 volunteers had open-label psilocybin in a third session, and MacLean's 35 Study 1 volunteers would include at least five of them (editors' inference).

inconsistency.note: In the trial that supplied 35 of the 52 volunteers, the randomized comparison found no difference in any personality factor (no values printed), while the pooled within-person analysis found a rise in Openness; and the two papers disagree on whether the change followed the experience (mystical score r = 0.42 in the volunteers; no peak-experience score related to Openness in the patients). Small groups and different designs may explain part of this; nothing resolves it.

indirectness.note: The question is whether psilocybin changes personality; the evidence is self-ratings only, with no behaviour and no ratings of personality by others, in selected volunteers (high baseline Openness, spiritually active) and in patients with treatment-resistant depression, in supported clinical or laboratory settings.

imprecision.note: 52 and 19 people; the main change has p = 0.023 and the lasting change p = 0.0503 in a subgroup of 30; a few large individual rises carry much of the mean (about +1.3 without the three largest, editors' approximate calculation); the randomized comparison prints no values, so its precision cannot be judged.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: neither paper mentions a registration or analysis plan; the 2006 trial did publish its null personality result.

grade.reasoning: The personality estimates are before-and-after changes within the same people, not comparisons between randomized conditions, so they are rated as observational and start low; rated down two levels for risk of bias and one each for inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether psilocybin changes personality: that self-rated Openness was a few points higher after than before in these two samples is reported in the statement, not rated as an effect of the drug. Counted once: the 2006 trial supplied 35 of MacLean's 52 volunteers, so its null comparison and MacLean's rise come largely from the same people; the patient study is from a London team that includes MacLean's first author, and its Openness rise points the same way under different conditions. Status contested: the before-and-after rises point one way, and the one randomized comparison, the subgroup on which the lasting change rests and the two papers' disagreement about the experience point the other; the debate box sets out both sides. Neither paper checked a change against behaviour.

debate.question: Does psilocybin change personality traits such as Openness, or do the before-and-after rises in self-ratings come from other things: expectations, improving mood, retesting or who volunteers?
debate.evidence_yes: In 52 healthy volunteers pooled from two double-blind laboratory trials, self-rated Openness was 2.8 T points higher 1 to 2 months after a high-dose psilocybin session (p = 0.023), while the other four domains, measured with the same questionnaire, retesting and setting, did not change detectably, and Openness did not change after a first session of placebo, methylphenidate or a low psilocybin dose (30 people, p = 0.48). The rise was larger the more mystical the session (r = 0.42) and concentrated in the 30 who had a 'complete mystical experience' (+5.7), whose screening Openness did not differ from the others', and in them it was still 4.2 points above screening at about 16 months (MacLean et al., 2011). Under different conditions, in 19 patients with treatment-resistant depression in an open-label study by a London team, Openness rose 4.9 points at 3 months; this rise did not differ between patients whose depression responded and those whose did not and did not correlate with depression change, which the authors read as an effect beyond improved mood, and it was more than three times the average change they computed from antidepressant trials (d 0.44 against 0.13), a comparison across separate studies (Erritzoe et al., 2018).
debate.evidence_no: Neither study compared personality change with a control condition: MacLean et al. tested the change after the high-dose session and the change after a first session without it separately, never against each other, and Erritzoe et al. had no control group. In the trial that supplied 35 of MacLean's 52 volunteers, the randomized comparison (15 given psilocybin first against 15 given methylphenidate first) found no difference in any personality factor at 2 months, and the methylphenidate-first group did not change after its own psilocybin session (no values printed; Griffiths et al., 2006, as its checked study card reports). The lasting change rests on p = 0.0503 in a subgroup defined by what happened in the session, and the change for all participants at follow-up was not reported; about a third of individual changes were below zero, and without the three largest rises the mean would be about +1.3 (editors' approximate reading of the figure). The volunteers were unpaid, mostly spiritually active, highly educated people whose Openness was already about 1.3 to 1.5 SDs above the norm, recruited by a study framed around sacramental use, who could probably tell when they had the high dose; expectations were not measured. In the patients, Neuroticism, Extraversion and Conscientiousness started far from the norms and moved towards them, as regression and lifting mood would predict, and the authors say it is hard to infer that these changes are traits rather than states. The two papers disagree on whether the change followed the experience.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether behaviour changed: all personality scores are self-reports, and no paper read related them to behaviour or to ratings by people who know the participants (the 2006 trial's observer ratings of behaviour and attitudes were not linked to personality scores). Whether changes last beyond about 16 months in the volunteers or 3 months in the patients. Whether the findings apply to people who are not volunteers for psilocybin research, to use outside a clinic or laboratory, or to other psychedelics: both studies gave psilocybin with preparation and support.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). After psilocybin with preparation and support, people rated themselves a few points more open to experience 1 to 3 months later, in two small studies, and patients with depression also rated themselves less anxious and more sociable as their mood improved. That psilocybin itself changed their personality is not shown: neither study compared the change with a control condition, the one randomized comparison in these trials found no difference, about a third of the volunteers scored lower afterwards, and no study read checked the scores against what people do. The rise more than a year later rests on a borderline result in a subgroup.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial comparing psilocybin with an active placebo that people cannot easily tell apart, with personality, self-rated and rated by people who know the participant, as a pre-registered outcome at baseline and at 1, 6 and at least 12 months, expectations measured beforehand, all five domains analysed for everyone randomized, depression change as a covariate in patients, and a measure of behaviour; repeated in people not selected for spiritual interest or high Openness.
